You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 4 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'P-SSHI-LargeBleed': duplicate: same structure as an earlier design (c0042); nothing new was simulated. Values are tuned automatically, so propose a different structure.

Design 2 'Doubler-SSHI': failed the screen and was not tuned (topology 852e73d8fd19).

what this means:
- with the output fixed at 4.5 V, the net power delivered covers only -16 % of the load's need on S2 (heavy load), -77 % of the load's need on S4 (weak excitation), -36 % of the load's need on S6 (Cp +20 %, hot) (best of the value presets tried)

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor node (RL) from a piezo transducer.
    *   Targets: $V_{avg} \ge 4.5\text{V}$, $V_{max} \le 5.5\text{V}$, $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$, $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$, $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Piezo: $I_p = 60\mu\text{A}$ (nominal), $f = 100\text{Hz}$, $C_p = 25\text{nF}$. $V_{oc} \approx 3.8\text{V}$.
    *   Constraint: Output range $4.5\text{V}$ to $5.5\text{V}$ is narrow.
    *   Current Best: `P-SSHI` (score 40.40). It delivers enough power (S2, S4, S6 screens are very high), but it's *too* powerful for S3, S1, S5 (exceeds 5.5V) and fails S4 startup (though the screen says it's powerful, the tuned results say it settles at 3.77V. Wait, check `P-SSHI` S4 results: $V_{avg} = 3.77\text{V}$. But the screen says it delivers 2260% of needed power. This is a contradiction).

    *Wait, let's look closer at `P-SSHI` [c0041]:*
    S1: $V_{avg} = 5.57\text{V}$ (FAIL $V_{max}$)
    S2: $V_{avg} = 5.08\text{V}$ (OK)
    S3: $V_{avg} = 12.2\text{V}$ (FAIL $V_{max}$)
    S4: $V_{avg} = 3.77\text{V}$ (FAIL $V_{min}$)
    S5: $V_{avg} = 6.09\text{V}$ (FAIL $V_{max}$)
    S6: $V_{avg} = 4.71\text{V}$ (OK)
    Screen S4: $97.4\mu\text{W}$ delivered, $4.31\mu\text{W}$ needed.
    Why does it settle at 3.77V if it provides $97\mu\text{W}$?
    Ah, the screen is done with `out` fixed at 4.5V. If the circuit can't actually *reach* 4.5V due to diode drops or voltage divider effects, it will fail. But here it's SSHI. The P-SSHI typically boosts.
    Wait, looking at the P-SSHI topology in [c0041]:
    `D1 pzp out`, `D2 pzn out`, `D3 0 pzp`, `D4 0 pzn` (Full Bridge Rectifier)
    `L1 pzp n1`, `S1 n1 pzn`, `G1 SYNC` (SSHI inversion loop).
    This is a standard Parallel-SSHI. The inductor $L1$ and switch $S1$ perform the inversion of $C_p$.

    Wait, the diode bridge is:
    D1: pzp -> out
    D2: pzn -> out
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    This means current always flows into `out`. If $V_{out}$ is $4.5\text{V}$, $V_{pzp}$ must reach $4.5 + 0.25 = 4.75\text{V}$ for D1 to conduct.
    The open circuit voltage of the piezo is $3.8\text{V}$. SSHI boosts the effective voltage by flipping $C_p$ charge.
    In S4, $I_p = 40\mu\text{A}$ (weak). $V_{oc} \approx 2.5\text{V}$.
    The problem is likely that the boost isn't enough or the loss is too high at low excitation.

    S3: $V_{avg} = 12.2\text{V}$ (Too high).
    S1, S5: $V_{avg} > 5.5\text{V}$ (Too high).
    S4: $V_{avg} = 3.77\text{V}$ (Too low).
    S2, S6: OK.

    We need to clamp the output voltage at 5.5V and ensure it can reach 4.5V in the worst case (S4).
    The DZ33 Zener diode is available. It breaks down at 3.3V. That's too low for a $4.5\text{V}$ output.
    Wait, I can't use a single DZ33 to clamp at 5.5V. I'd need two in series? (3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6V, still not 5.5V).
    Wait, I can use a Zener in a different way or a different clamping strategy.
    Actually, if $V_{out}$ is too high, the easiest way is to add a shunt (bleeder) or a regulator. A bleeder resistor (Rbleed) was tried in [c0090] but the score was much worse. Why? Because it likely wasted too much power, preventing S1, S2, S4 from reaching 4.5V.

    Let's reconsider the P-SSHI. The voltage $V_{out}$ is determined by the balance of harvested power and load power.
    $P_{harvested} = P_{load} + P_{bleed}$.
    In S3, $P_{harvested}$ is very high and $P_{load}$ is very low ($R_L = 10\text{M}\Omega$), so $V_{out}$ skyrockets.
    In S4, $P_{harvested}$ is low and $P_{load}$ is moderate ($R_L = 4.7\text{M}\Omega$), so $V_{out}$ is too low.

    To fix S3 (overvoltage), we need a way to limit $V_{out}$. A Zener diode is the standard way. But DZ33 is 3.3V.
    Is there any other way to limit voltage? A shunt regulator.
    What if we use a different SSHI topology?
    Maybe a "Buck-boost" like SSHI or a different rectifier?
    Actually, the most robust way to limit voltage to 5.5V without a 5.5V Zener is a shunt that becomes conductive above 5.5V. But we only have DZ33.

    Wait, can I use a Zener to create a reference for a switch? No, the SYNC is ideal and doesn't use a reference voltage from the circuit.

    Let's think about the P-SSHI again. The issue is the wide range of $I_p$ and $R_L$.
    If $V_{out}$ is too high, we need to discard energy.
    If $V_{out}$ is too low, we need to harvest more efficiently.

    Could we use a different rectifier?
    Standard FBR: $V_{out} \approx V_{oc} - 2V_d$.
    SSHI: $V_{out}$ can be much higher.

    What if we use a "Current-Limited" SSHI?
    Or maybe a different inductor-switch placement.

    Let's try to improve the P-SSHI by adding a more clever way to limit voltage.
    If $V_{out}$ is too high, we can increase the "bleed".
    What if the bleed is non-linear?
    A DZ33 Zener diode from `out` to `0` will clamp $V_{out}$ to 3.3V. That's below our 4.5V minimum.
    But what if we put the Zener in series with another diode?
    $V_{clamp} = 3.3\text{V} + 0.7\text{V} = 4.0\text{V}$. Still too low.
    Two Zener diodes in series? $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6\text{V}$. That's close to 5.5V, but maybe too high.

    Wait, what if we change the SSHI to a different version?
    Standard P-SSHI:
    Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with $C_p$.
    When $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate, flipping the voltage.
    The flipped charge is then pushed into the rectifier.

    Let's look at the failing S4 again. $V_{out} = 3.77\text{V}$.
    $V_{oc} \approx 2.5\text{V}$.
    The P-SSHI should boost this. The reason it might fail is if the $t_{on}$ is not optimized or if the $C_{out}$ is too small.
    In [c0041], $C_1 = 613\text{nF}$. This is quite small. A larger $C_{out}$ would reduce ripple and potentially help stability, but the average voltage is the main issue.

    Wait, let's try a different approach for the overvoltage in S3.
    If the P-SSHI is too efficient, we can use a "lossy" rectifier or a shunt.
    But a simple resistor bleed is either too much (S4 fails) or too little (S3 fails).
    Is there a way to make the harvest less efficient when $V_{out}$ is high?
    Not with the given components.

    Wait! Let's try a different SSHI variant.
    The "S-SSHI" (Series-SSHI) often has different characteristics.
    In S-SSHI, the inductor is in series with the rectifier.

    Actually, let's try to refine the P-SSHI. The P-SSHI in [c0041] is:
    D1, D2, D3, D4 = Full Bridge
    L1, S1 = Inversion loop
    C1 = Storage

    What if we use a "Half-Bridge" SSHI to reduce diode drops?
    If the piezo is centered (pzp and pzn), we can't really avoid two diode drops unless we use a virtual ground.
    But we can use a "Voltage Doubler" style rectifier.

    Wait, the `Doubler-SSHI` (Design 2) failed the screen. Let's look at its topology:
    D1: pzp -> n1
    C1: n1 -> 0
    D2: pzn -> out
    D3: n1 -> out
    C2: out -> 0
    L1: pzp -> n2
    S1: n2 -> pzn
    This is a charge pump.

    Let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" but with a larger storage capacitor and maybe a different inductor value.
    Wait, the "Automatic tuning" already tried 48 evaluations. The topology is the key.

    Is there another way to clamp $V_{out}$?
    What if we use a Zener as a "crowbar" that doesn't fully clamp but just limits the peak?
    No, DZ33 will clamp to 3.3V.

    Let's think about the "P-SSHI" again. It's the best so far.
    Failing S3 (max voltage), S4 (min voltage), S5 (max voltage).
    If we can't clamp the voltage, can we lower the efficiency specifically when $V_{out}$ is high?
    That's hard.
    What if we use a different inductor-switch configuration to make the boost less aggressive?

    Actually, look at the `P-SSHI` [c0041] results:
    S1: 5.57V (just over 5.5)
    S2: 5.08V (perfect)
    S3: 12.2V (way over)
    S4: 3.77V (too low)
    S5: 6.09V (over)
    S6: 4.71V (perfect)
    The problem is mainly S3 and S4.
    S3 has $I_p = 120\mu\text{A}$ and $R_L = 10\text{M}\Omega$.
    S4 has $I_p = 40\mu\text{A}$ and $R_L = 4.7\text{M}\Omega$.
    The P-SSHI is *very* sensitive to the source strength.

    What if we use a different inductor value or a different $t_{on}$?
    The tuner already tried that.
    Wait, the tuner optimizes $C_1$ and $t_{on}$.
    Maybe the inductor $L_1$ is too large? (0.01H).
    If we change the topology slightly, we might get a different response.

    Let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" using the SYNC switches?
    We have up to 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.
    A synchronous rectifier would eliminate diode drops.
    For example:
    Switch S1: pzp -> out
    Switch S2: pzn -> out
    Switch S3: 0 -> pzp
    Switch S4: 0 -> pzn
    This would be a full-bridge synchronous rectifier.
    But we only have 2 SYNCs.
    We can use one SYNC to control two switches if they are tied to the same "ctrl".
    Wait, "S switch... 'ctrl': id of a SYNC". This means multiple switches can be controlled by one SYNC.
    S1, S2 can be `ctrl: G1`, and S3, S4 can be `ctrl: G2`.
    G1: closes at positive peak (edges: pos).
    G2: closes at negative peak (edges: neg).
    Wait, the SYNC closes for `ton` seconds. This is a very short pulse.
    A synchronous rectifier needs to be closed for the *whole* half-cycle.
    The SYNC is designed for the $L-C_p$ inversion pulse (very short), not for rectification.
    So we must use diodes for rectification.

    Back to the P-SSHI. How to limit $V_{out}$?
    If we can't use a Zener, and a bleed resistor is too blunt, what else?
    Maybe a "parallel" storage capacitor? No, that doesn't change $V_{avg}$.

    What if we use a different rectifier? A "Half-Wave" rectifier?
    D1: pzp -> out
    D2: 0 -> pzp
    This would harvest half the energy, potentially fixing S3, but making S4 worse.

    Wait, look at the P-SSHI again. The "P" means the inductor is in parallel with $C_p$.
    What if we use the "S-SSHI" (Series-SSHI)?
    In S-SSHI:
    $C_p$ is in series with the inductor and a switch.
    Wait, the standard SSHI has the inductor-switch loop and the rectifier.
    The "P-SSHI" (Parallel) is usually:
    Piezo $C_p$ in parallel with ($L$ and $S$ in series).
    The rectifier is then connected to the piezo.
    This is what [c0041] is.

    Is there a way to reduce the output voltage?
